newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela urges SAfricans to come clean on apartheid.
newsitem.headline: Mandela urges SAfricans to come clean on apartheid.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela urged apartheid leaders on Saturday to come clean on their roles in upholding racial segregation which ended in 1994 with the country's first all-race elections.
In a veiled reference to former white presidents F.W. de Klerk and P.W. Botha, Mandela said they could not avoid responsibility for human rights abuses committed under apartheid.

"The people who led apartheid cannot avoid accepting responsibility for acts which were seen as crimes in the eyes of the entire world," Mandela told a memorial service for five slain African National Congress (ANC) members killed by police in the late 1980s.

"We also need to look at the perpetrators of these crimes, from the people who pulled the trigger to those who gave the orders, as well as those who created and maintained the system which allowed such unspeakable violations of human rights to take place," he said.

Six policemen are seeking amnesty from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which was set up to uncover crimes and human rights abuses under apartheid, for the murders of the four men and one women to whom the service was dedicated.
Mandela told an audience of 4,000 people his ruling ANC would support party members for "bona fide actions" committed during the liberation struggle against apartheid.

"On our part as the liberation movement, we have acknowledged that mistakes were committed in the cause of the struggle. As leaders, we are prepared to stand by the cadres who took bona fide actions."
The ANC earlier this month said senior members would apply for amnesty before the May 10 deadline. Up to 300 members of the ANC have applied so far, including Defence Minister Joe Modise.
Mandela called on poltical leaders, their parties and armed force members across the political divide to testify before the commission.
"The time is now for those who led the country into the political wilderness to admit the error of their ways. We call on them to join us in building a better future," Mandela said.
